name: STM32G431CBT6
title: Arm Cortex-M4 170 MHz microcontroller with FPU, 32 to 128 KB flash, 32 KB SRAM, rich analog, 1.71 V to 3.6 V
summary: A Cortex-M4 microcontroller with a single-precision FPU, DSP instructions and an MPU, running at up to 170 MHz from a 1.71 V to 3.6 V supply. It carries 32, 64 or 128 KB of flash with ECC and 32 KB of SRAM, a CORDIC and a filter accelerator, two 12-bit ADCs, four DAC channels, four fast comparators, three op amps with PGA and a reference buffer. Communication covers FDCAN, USB full-speed device, USB Type-C power delivery, three I2C, four USART/UART plus an LPUART, three SPI and a SAI, in packages from 32 to 100 pins.

operation.text: The Cortex-M4 runs Arm's full single-precision float and DSP instruction sets. The ART accelerator lets code run from flash with no wait states up to the top clock. The MPU guards up to 8 regions of 32 bytes to 4 GB, each split into 8 subregions; an RTOS normally manages it, and it can be left off.

Option bytes set readout protection in three levels: level 0 none, level 1 no flash access while debug is connected or the part boots from RAM or the bootloader, level 2 debug, RAM boot and bootloader selection shut off for good. Write protection blocks erase and programming of an area. PCROP makes an area execute-only for the CPU; an option bit picks whether it is wiped when RDP goes from level 1 back to 0. A securable area can be locked after boot so that it answers every access with an error until the next reset. ECC corrects single and detects double errors, and logs the failing address. 1 KB of OTP, in bank 1, can be written once and never erased.

SRAM1 (16 KB) sits at 0x2000 0000 and is reached over the system bus or the I-Code/D-Code bus. SRAM2 (6 KB) at 0x2000 4000 is on the system bus and can be kept through Stop and Standby. CCM SRAM (10 KB) at 0x1000 0000 is on the I-Code/D-Code bus for full speed, and is also mirrored at 0x2000 5800 so that the CPU and both DMAs see it right after SRAM1 and SRAM2. The first 16 KB of SRAM and the CCM SRAM have hardware parity.

A 32-bit multi-AHB matrix links the masters (CPU I-bus, D-bus and S-bus, DMA1, DMA2) to flash through the accelerator, SRAM1, CCM SRAM, SRAM2 and the AHB1 and AHB2 peripherals, so several fast peripherals can work at once.

At start-up BOOT0 and the nBOOT1 option bit choose user flash, system memory or embedded SRAM. BOOT0 comes from the PB8-BOOT0 pin, or from the nBOOT0 option bit when nBOOT_SEL says so, which frees the pin as a GPIO. The bootloader in system memory reprograms flash over USART, I2C, SPI or USB DFU.

A 24-bit CORDIC engine in circular and hyperbolic, rotation and vectoring modes computes cosine, sine, atan, atan2, atanh, sinh, cosh, square root, modulus and natural log. Precision is selectable up to 20 bits at 4 bits per clock, with 16-bit or 32-bit fixed-point data. Results can be read the moment they are ready, and DMA serves both directions.

The filter accelerator has a 16 x 16-bit multiplier, a 24+2-bit accumulator and 256 x 16-bit local memory holding up to three buffers (two inputs, one output) that can be circular, with a watermark to cut interrupt overhead. It runs FIR and IIR (direct form 1) filters with 16-bit data, fed over AHB and DMA.
The CRC unit uses a configurable polynomial and size. It can check flash integrity at run time against a signature made at link time, which is one way to meet EN/IEC 60335-1.

VDD (1.71 V to 3.6 V) feeds the I/Os, the regulator and the system analog blocks. VDDA (1.62 V to 3.6 V, with higher minimums per block in the operating conditions) feeds the ADCs, DACs, comparators, op amps and VREFBUF; it is independent of VDD and is best tied to VDD when those blocks are unused. VBAT (1.55 V to 3.6 V) keeps the RTC, the LSE and the backup registers alive through a power switch when VDD is absent. VREF+ is the ADC and DAC reference and the VREFBUF output: equal to VDDA when VDDA < 2 V, between 2 V and VDDA otherwise. VREF- is bonded to VSSA. In the 32-pin packages VREF+ and VDDA share one pin and VREFBUF cannot be used.

VDD takes one 100 nF per VDD pin plus one 4.7 µF; VDDA takes 10 nF plus 1 µF; VREF+ takes 100 nF plus 1 µF. All are ceramic and go as close as possible to their supply pair, or under it on the far side of the board. The VDDA capacitor in particular is a good-quality ceramic right at the chip.

A brown-out reset works in every mode except Shutdown and holds the part in reset while VDD is under the threshold, so no external reset circuit is needed. The lowest level is 1.71 V at power-on; higher BOR levels come from option bytes. The PVD compares VDD with a programmable threshold and can interrupt on either crossing. A peripheral voltage monitor checks VDDA against fixed thresholds (PVM1 for COMP/ADC, PVM2 for OPAMP/DAC).

A main regulator serves Run and Sleep, a low-power one serves Stop, Low-power sleep and Low-power run; in Standby and Shutdown both are off and their outputs high-impedance. The core voltage scales with frequency: Range 1 boost mode up to 170 MHz, Range 1 normal mode up to 150 MHz, Range 2 up to 26 MHz.

Sleep stops only the CPU. Low-power run executes from flash or SRAM on the low-power regulator with the CPU at 2 MHz at most. Stop keeps SRAM and registers but stops every core-domain clock, the PLL, HSI16 and HSE, while LSE or LSI and optionally the RTC run; peripherals able to wake the part can turn HSI16 on to handle the event. Standby turns the core domain off but keeps BOR; SRAM and registers are lost except the RTC domain, standby logic and optionally SRAM2, and each I/O can get a pull-up, pull-down or nothing. Shutdown is lower still: no BOR, no supply monitoring, LSI off. Standby and Shutdown end on NRST, an IWDG reset, a WKUP pin edge or an RTC event; Standby also on an LSE failure.

Under and after reset the I/Os sit in analog state with the Schmitt trigger off to save current, and the reset pull-up is turned off when the reset comes from inside. NRST has a fixed internal pull-up RPU; a 0.1 µF capacitor on NRST close to the chip guards against stray resets, and whatever drives the pin must take it under VIL(NRST) max.

VBAT can come from a battery, a supercapacitor, or VDD. The part switches to it by itself when VDD goes away, and it keeps the RTC with the LSE, the backup registers and three tamper pins running. An internal charger can charge a VBAT cell from VDD through 5 kΩ or 1.5 kΩ. On VBAT alone neither external interrupts nor RTC events bring the part back.

SYSCLK comes from the HSE (4 to 48 MHz crystal or ceramic resonator, or an external clock in bypass), from HSI16 (16 MHz RC, trimmable) or from the PLL (up to 170 MHz, fed by HSE or HSI16). HSI48 clocks USB and the RNG. The RTC runs from the LSE (32.768 kHz crystal with four drive levels, or bypass) or the LSI (32 kHz RC, ±5 %), which also clocks the IWDG. I2S, USART, I2C, LPTIM, ADC, SAI and RNG can use their own kernel clocks. The clock security system moves SYSCLK to HSI16 if the HSE fails and can flag an LSE failure. MCO puts out an internal clock; LSCO puts out LSI or LSE in every low-power mode. AHB and both APB buses run up to 170 MHz.

For the HSE crystal, CL1 and CL2 are high-quality high-frequency ceramics, typically 5 pF to 20 pF and normally equal. The crystal's rated load is their series value plus the pin and board capacitance, roughly 10 pF. Crystal and capacitors go as close to the oscillator pins as possible to keep distortion and start-up time down; REXT depends on the crystal. The LSE crystal takes no resistor between OSC32_IN and OSC32_OUT, and fitting one is not allowed. ST application note AN2867 covers crystal choice.

Each GPIO can be a push-pull or open-drain output, a floating, pulled-up or pulled-down input, or an alternate function; most pins also carry analog functions. The ports sit on AHB2 for fast toggling, and a lock sequence can freeze a pin's configuration. FT pins tolerate 5 V, TT pins 3.6 V, FT_c pins (UCPD) 5.5 V; the 'a' option adds an analog switch on VDDA, 'f' Fm+ drive, 'u' USB, 'c' and 'd' USB Type-C and dead-battery functions. Outputs drive ±8 mA, or ±20 mA with relaxed VOL/VOH, within the ΣIVDD and ΣIVSS limits.

A floating input can drift to a middle level or toggle with outside noise and draw current. Unused pins should be put in analog mode or held at a defined level by a pull resistor or by making them outputs. PB8-BOOT0 left open is best taken out of analog mode after start-up.

PC13, PC14 and PC15 run from the backup power switch, which sinks only about 3 mA: as outputs they are good for 2 MHz into 30 pF at most and must not source current. Their function after a backup-domain power-up depends on RTC registers that a system reset leaves alone.

Two DMA controllers with six channels each (12 in all) move data between peripherals and memory, memory and memory, or peripheral and peripheral, up to 65536 items per transfer. Priorities are four software levels with channel order breaking ties; transfer sizes are byte, half-word or word, with packing; circular buffers are supported; half-transfer, complete and error flags share one interrupt per channel. The DMAMUX routes any peripheral request to any channel, synchronously with events if wanted, and includes a request generator.

The NVIC handles up to 71 maskable channels plus the 16 Cortex-M4 lines, with 16 priority levels, tail chaining and late-arrival handling. The EXTI has 39 edge-detector lines that raise interrupts or events and wake the part from Stop; up to 86 GPIOs map onto its 16 external lines, and pulses shorter than the internal clock period are still caught.

Two SAR ADCs give 12 bits with built-in calibration at up to 4 Msps (6.66 Msps at 6 bits), sampling down to about 25 ns. Inputs are single-ended or differential. A sequencer runs regular and injected groups, single, continuous or discontinuous, triggered by timers or external signals, with DMA. Hardware oversampling raises the result to 16 bits; there are per-channel offsets and sampling times, analog watchdogs that can trigger timers, and gain and offset compensation. Fast channels are ADCx_IN1 to IN5; all other inputs are slow channels with lower RAIN limits.

The temperature sensor gives a voltage linear in temperature on ADC1_IN16; its offset varies part to part, so readings need the factory values TS_CAL1 (30 °C) and TS_CAL2 (110 °C), taken at VDDA = VREF+ = 3.0 V. VREFINT, a bandgap on ADC1_IN18, is measured on each part at 30 °C and stored as VREFINT_CAL. VBAT is read on ADC1_IN17 through an internal divide-by-3 bridge.

Four 12-bit DAC channels: two buffered outputs to pins at up to 1 Msps and two internal unbuffered channels at up to 15 Msps for the comparators and op amps. Features include 8- or 12-bit data, buffer offset calibration, noise, triangle and sawtooth generation, dual simultaneous conversion, DMA, external triggers from timer update outputs, and a sample-and-hold low-power mode with an internal or external hold capacitor.

The reference buffer drives VREF+ at 2.048 V, 2.5 V or 2.9 V (VRS bits) for the ADCs, DACs and outside parts; its load needs 0.5 µF to 1.5 µF including a low-ESR 100 nF. With the buffer off, an external reference can feed VREF+. In packages where VREF+ is bonded to VDDA the buffer is not available. If VDDA is too low for the chosen level, the buffer drops into degraded mode and follows VDDA.

Four rail-to-rail comparators with programmable hysteresis compare against an I/O, a DAC channel, or VREFINT and its 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4 steps. Each can wake the part from Stop, interrupt, and drive timer breaks and blanking.

Three op amps, rail-to-rail in and out, about 13 MHz GBW, usable as followers, standalone amplifiers with every terminal on pins, or PGAs with non-inverting gains 2 to 64 and inverting gains -1 to -63 from internal resistors. Their outputs can go straight to an ADC channel internally.

TIM1 and TIM8 are 16-bit advanced timers: four channels with complementary outputs, programmable dead time, break inputs and PWM freeze in debug, for motor control. TIM2 (32-bit) and TIM3, TIM4 (16-bit) have four channels each and quadrature encoder inputs. TIM15 has two channels with one complementary output, TIM16 and TIM17 one channel and one complementary output. TIM6 and TIM7 are basic timers that mainly trigger the DACs. LPTIM1 keeps counting in Stop from LSE, LSI or an external clock and can wake the part. Timers link to each other for synchronisation or chaining.

The IWDG (12-bit down-counter, 8-bit prescaler) runs from the LSI and keeps going in Stop and Standby; it can be started by hardware or software through option bytes. The WWDG (7-bit) runs from the APB clock and gives an early-warning interrupt. SysTick is a 24-bit auto-reload down-counter for an RTOS.

The BCD calendar RTC has subseconds, two alarms, a 17-bit wakeup timer, smooth calibration at 0.95 ppm steps, a 50/60 Hz reference input and timestamps on a pin, a tamper event or a switch to VBAT. It runs from LSE, LSI or HSE/32; on the LSE it works in VBAT and every low-power mode, on the LSI it stops in VBAT and Shutdown. Sixteen 32-bit backup registers survive every low-power mode and VBAT; up to three tamper pins and five internal tamper sources erase them and can wake the part.
TIM17 channel 1 supplies the carrier and TIM16 channel 1 the envelope; IRTIM combines them onto IR_OUT on PB9 or PA13.

Three I2C controllers do Standard (100 kbit/s), Fast (400 kbit/s) and Fast-mode Plus (1 Mbit/s with 20 mA drive), master and slave, 7- and 10-bit addresses, with SMBus 2.0 and PMBus 1.1 support, analog and digital noise filters, an independent kernel clock and wakeup from Stop on address match. The I2C kernel clock has to be above the minimum in its table for the timings to hold.

USART1 to USART3 and UART4 handle asynchronous, multiprocessor, single-wire half-duplex, IrDA and LIN, with CTS/RTS and RS-485 driver enable; the USARTs add Smartcard (ISO 7816) and SPI-like synchronous modes. Each has 8-deep transmit and receive FIFOs, an independent kernel clock and wakeup from Stop. The LPUART can receive at up to 9600 baud from the 32.768 kHz LSE alone while the part is in Stop.

Three SPIs reach 75 Mbit/s as master and 41 Mbit/s as slave, with 4- to 16-bit frames, NSS pulse and TI modes and hardware CRC. SPI2 and SPI3 can instead be half-duplex I2S at 8 kHz to 192 kHz, with an MCLK output of 256 x Fs in master mode. The SAI has two sub-blocks, each with an 8-word FIFO, covering I2S, MSB- or LSB-justified, PCM/DSP, TDM and AC'97, an SPDIF output, and as many as 16 slots.
One CAN controller meets ISO 11898-1 (CAN 2.0 A and B) and CAN FD 1.0, with 1 KB of message RAM for filters, receive FIFOs and buffers and transmit buffers.

A USB 2.0 full-speed device with built-in PHY, DP pull-up, LPM and battery charging detection (BCD 1.2), with up to 1 KB of packet memory. It needs an accurate 48 MHz clock: the PLL from an HSE crystal, or HSI48 trimmed by the clock recovery system from USB start-of-frame packets, which allows crystal-less operation between -15 and 85 °C. No series resistors are needed on DP and DM. Full USB electrical performance needs VDD ≥ 3.0 V.

The USB Type-C and Power Delivery controller (Type-C 1.2, PD 3.0) has switchable Rp and Rd on its CC pins (PB6/UCPD1_CC1 and PB4/UCPD1_CC2), dead-battery support on the DBCC pins, fast role swap, and handles PD message framing, 4b5b coding and CRC in hardware. It keeps listening for PD messages in Stop. Sink-only use needs VDD 3.0 V to 3.6 V; source and sink needs 3.135 V to 3.465 V.

The SWJ-DP serves JTAG (5 pins) or serial-wire debug on two pins (SWDIO on PA13, SWCLK on PA14), switched by a sequence on TMS. After reset PA13, PA14, PA15, PB3 and PB4 are in their debug functions with pull-ups on PA13, PA15 and PB4 and a pull-down on PA14. The ETM streams instruction and data trace through TRACECK and TRACED0 to TRACED3 to an external trace port analyzer.

Voltages are referred to VSS. Min and max values are production tested on every part at 25 °C and at the top of the temperature range; values from characterization, design or simulation say so in a note and are mean ± 3σ. Typical values are at 25 °C and VDD = VDDA = 3 V. Typical ADC accuracy is the level 95 % of parts meet (mean ± 2σ) over temperature. Pin parameters are measured with a 50 pF load.

The maximum junction temperature is 105 °C for suffix 6 and 130 °C for suffix 3. Thermal resistances (junction to ambient, case and board) for each package are in the thermal table; the junction temperature follows from ambient plus dissipation times ΘJA, where dissipation is the internal power IDD x VDD plus the output-pin power. Junction-ambient figures follow JESD51-2 (still air).

The UFQFPN parts have an exposed pad underneath to be soldered to ground.
